sourceVariantTitle: Asteroids: A Question of Risk, Not Panic
scoreRule: One point per correct answer; ten points maximum. Provisional local result only.
description: New English B2 independent assessment on interpreting risk, scientific estimates, planetary defence and public communication.

tabs.title: Reading Scientific Claims
tabs.description: Consider how estimates, headlines and evidence should be interpreted.

tabs.title: Evidence and Limitations
tabs.description: Distinguish an experiment's result from what it can prove.

tabs.title: Decisions and Communication
tabs.description: Transfer the ideas into realistic decisions.

questions.q: A headline announces that a small asteroid will come 'near Earth'. What information should a cautious reader ask for first?
choices: The number of people who have already shared the headline.
Whether a space agency has named the asteroid after its discoverer.
The actual estimated distance and whether the predicted path intersects Earth.
The size of the telescope that first took its picture.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one separates a close approach from a possible collision and warns against interpreting 'near' without a distance.

questions.q: Two published risk figures for the same asteroid differ after several nights of observation. Which explanation best fits the article?
choices: The asteroid must have suddenly changed direction between observations.
The later estimate may reflect more precise calculations based on additional evidence.
The earlier calculation was necessarily dishonest or entirely arbitrary.
The probability must remain unchanged until the object becomes visible to the naked eye.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two explains that repeated observations refine an orbit and may change the reported estimate without implying random guessing.

questions.q: What is the most reasonable lesson to draw from the changing estimates for 2024 YR4?
choices: An increasing percentage proves that an asteroid is moving faster towards Earth.
The first reported risk is usually more reliable than later telescope observations.
Space agencies should publish only predictions that never need revising.
An estimate can temporarily increase before new data make a possible impact unlikely.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three describes the rise and subsequent fall in 2024 YR4's estimated impact chance as more observations became available.

questions.q: Why would the article regard a risk figure without its uncertainty as potentially misleading?
choices: The number may sound more definite than the available observations justify.
The number is useful only if it is presented in kilometres.
The risk is determined by public concern rather than scientific observations.
The figure is meaningless until the asteroid has actually approached Earth.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two explains that repeated observations refine an orbit and may change the reported estimate without implying random guessing.

questions.q: A student claims that DART proved any dangerous asteroid could be diverted. What does the article leave unresolved?
choices: Whether the spacecraft really reached the smaller object in the system.
Whether the impact had any effect on the length of Dimorphos's orbit.
Whether the method would work for objects of different structures and with different warning times.
Whether scientists had originally selected an object that was already threatening Earth.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four explains the limited significance of DART and the importance of an object's structure and the warning time available.

questions.q: What would be the greatest difficulty if scientists discovered a real impact risk only shortly before the event?
choices: There might not be sufficient time for a small change in course to prevent the encounter.
The object's orbit would no longer follow the laws of physics.
Scientists would be unable to send any observations to other countries.
An asteroid would automatically become too bright for optical telescopes.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four explains the limited significance of DART and the importance of an object's structure and the warning time available.

questions.q: Which response to the YR4 updates best reflects the author's view of scientific uncertainty?
choices: Treat the decrease in probability as evidence that earlier scientists had failed.
Explain why the estimates changed and what the new observations show.
Stop communicating with the public until every possible uncertainty disappears.
Present the largest recorded percentage as a permanent estimate.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three describes the rise and subsequent fall in 2024 YR4's estimated impact chance as more observations became available.

questions.q: An observatory has new measurements that contradict a widely shared asteroid headline. What should its public statement emphasise?
choices: A promise that no dangerous asteroid will ever approach Earth.
The media outlet's motives rather than the orbit itself.
A guarantee that future calculations will not change.
The newer evidence, the limits of the estimate and why the previous claim needs updating.
questions.explanation: Paragraph five presents careful observation, international cooperation and honest communication of uncertainty as central to planetary defence.

questions.q: A government can fund either more observations or a spectacular last-minute deflection demonstration. Which first step is most strongly supported here?
choices: Announce a guaranteed successful deflection before an object is discovered.
Improve detection and reliable information, so a later intervention could be planned in time.
Stop international data sharing until every country agrees on a warning.
Focus entirely on producing dramatic public images of spacecraft.
questions.explanation: Paragraph five presents careful observation, international cooperation and honest communication of uncertainty as central to planetary defence.

questions.q: Which sentence best preserves the article's conclusion without exaggerating either the danger or the solution?
choices: Every close approach should be treated as an immediate emergency.
Future spacecraft can make any collision physically impossible.
The rare possibility of an impact means observation is no longer necessary.
Asteroid hazards call for careful evidence, preparation and cooperation rather than panic or certainty.
questions.explanation: Paragraph five presents careful observation, international cooperation and honest communication of uncertainty as central to planetary defence.
